# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization is a family of techniques in blocky meshing that reduces the rendering load by reconstructing voxel geometry from triangles and removing faces that are adjacent to solid neighbors or occluded from the camera [S1, unofficial]. It solves the problem of naively rendering all six faces of every voxel, which wastes GPU bandwidth on hidden interior surfaces. It sets itself apart from [Greedy face merging](8935-greedy-face-merging.md) by operating on individual face visibility rather than merging adjacent coplanar faces, and from [Boolean Voxel Meshing](971-boolean-voxel-meshing.md) by typically relying on discrete neighbor checks or camera-relative tests rather than constructive solid geometry operations.

## Shared principles
The core mechanism across this family is the determination of face visibility before or during mesh generation. A face is considered visible if it separates a solid voxel from an empty space (or a transparent space, depending on the method) and is not occluded by other geometry. The primary optimization is the exclusion of "interior" faces—those shared between two adjacent solid voxels.

Mathematically, for a voxel at position $P$ with a face normal $\vec{n}$, the face is culled if the neighbor at $P + \vec{n}$ is solid. In dynamic or camera-relative methods, visibility is further constrained by the camera's position and orientation. For example, backfaces are culled if the dot product of the face normal and the view direction is positive (assuming the view direction points from the camera to the object).

The output is a set of vertices and indices representing only the exposed surfaces. This reduces the primitive count from $6N$ (for $N$ voxels) to approximately $2N$ for dense volumes, as only the boundary faces are rendered [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)
A technique for dynamically updating a voxel chunk's internal state and face visibility when blocks are placed or removed. It uses neighbor checks to toggle shared faces without regenerating the entire mesh. It differs from [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by operating on discrete block indices and explicit face toggles rather than coverage masks, and from [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md) by focusing on logical state management rather than vertex buffer layout. Choose this for dynamic voxel worlds where blocks are frequently added or removed.

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
A method for removing hidden faces of partial voxel shapes (such as stairs, slabs, or custom geometries) by representing face coverage as a bit mask. It solves the problem where a boolean "solid/empty" flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. Unlike sibling methods that rely on coarse block visibility, this method operates at the sub-face granularity. Choose this when rendering non-cubic voxel shapes.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
A method for generating and maintaining dynamic, face-based meshes for voxel chunks by packing vertex attributes into compact 32-bit integers and managing buffer updates via a reusable vertex slot system. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and frequent GPU buffer uploads. Unlike [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md), which focuses on static placement, this method provides the underlying data structure and update logic for dynamic meshing. Choose this for performance-critical dynamic voxel engines.

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
This method optimizes voxel mesh generation by rejecting invisible faces in projection space and masking faces shared between neighboring voxels. It distinguishes itself from [Greedy Meshing](1776-greedy-meshing.md) by performing visibility culling per-voxel during geometry generation rather than post-processing a full mesh. Choose this when using geometry shaders or when explicit front/back orientation relative to the camera is required.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
Determines which discrete voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering by comparing the camera's current position and orientation against the previous frame's state. It operates by calculating screen-space projections relative to the player's position and culling invisible faces based on surface orientation. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on camera-relative coordinate transformation and explicit orientation flags. Choose this to avoid unnecessary computation when the view has not changed significantly.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
A fast display method for direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a 2D boundary tracing algorithm on axis-aligned slices to determine visibility from a fixed set of viewing directions. Choose this for direct volume rendering or when a point-based representation is acceptable.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
Filters mesh vertices and faces by projecting them into multiple camera views and checking if they fall within dilated binary masks, removing geometry not visible in any view. It differs from sibling methods by operating on explicit mesh geometry rather than voxel occupancy. Choose this when a set of reference images with associated segmentation or depth masks is available to define the visible region of interest.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
Culls mesh geometry by comparing projected vertex depths against reference depth maps rendered from multiple camera poses, classifying faces as seen, unseen, or forecast. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using explicit multi-view depth consistency checks. Choose this for cleaning up unbounded reconstructions or removing artifacts from multi-view stereo.

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
The foundational mesh generation optimization for voxel-based volume rendering that reduces the number of vertices sent to the GPU by skipping the rendering of voxel faces adjacent to existing neighboring voxels. It is distinguished from its siblings by its direct per-voxel neighbor lookup approach. Choose this as the standard baseline for static or semi-static voxel meshes.

#### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The process involves resetting the bitmask, creating mapped adjacent chunks for neighbor access, and iterating through all blocks to determine if they are buried. If all blocks in a chunk are buried, the mesh is marked as empty and generation is skipped. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set is skipped [S2, unofficial].

#### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw [S3, unofficial]. The first pass generates opaque faces between air/transparent blocks (testing for opaque blocks if transparent blocks exist, otherwise non-air). The second pass generates transparent faces only for blocks touching air, ignoring solid block types to avoid adding redundant faces between transparent and solid blocks [S3, unofficial].

#### Opacity-based Mesh Culling
Clips triangular faces if the opacity of all intersection points on that face is below 0.3, retaining only meshes meeting this criterion, which can reduce mesh count to 5% of the original [S4]. It also performs coordinate transformation to align the mesh with real-world scale and maps vertex coordinates to UV positions [S4].

## Background
The concept of removing interior polygons was introduced in the context of voxel-based procedural terrain generation, specifically in implementations resembling Minecraft [S1, unofficial]. Early engines instantiated full cube models for every block, rendering 12 triangles (6 sides) per cube even when only 2 triangles (1 side) were visible. The optimization involved reconstructing cubes from triangles and checking for solid neighbors; if a neighbor existed, the adjacent side was not rendered [S1, unofficial]. To further optimize, meshes of all cubes were combined into a single "chunk" mesh, though this introduced vertex count limits (e.g., ~65,000 vertices in Unity) [S1, unofficial]. The technique has since evolved to include dynamic updates, camera-relative culling, and handling of partial shapes and transparency.
